Final examination, badge and certificate when complete

modules.title: Networking Foundations for Security
modules.purpose:
A branch ticket says the core banking app is unreachable but the printer works. Before you can secure a network you need to be able to explain exactly how packets move through it. This module covers layer models, IP addressing and subnetting, switching, ARP and routing, TCP and UDP, and the DHCP, DNS, NAT and TLS services behind every connection, always with the security consequences in view. You finish by solving the ticket.

**To complete this module:** finish all five lessons and pass the lab (80%), including the written ticket resolution.
modules.prerequisiteKnowledge: Basic computer literacy and comfort with the command line. No prior networking knowledge is assumed; lesson 2 includes a subnetting refresher.
objectives: Map protocols and security controls to network layers
Calculate subnet boundaries and decide whether hosts share a subnet
Explain host forwarding decisions, ARP and longest-prefix routing
Interpret TCP and UDP behaviour, ports and connection states
Describe how DHCP, DNS, NAT/PAT and TLS work, how each is abused, and which logs each produces
Troubleshoot a connectivity fault from evidence and document the fix
assessmentCriteria: Predicts host and router forwarding decisions
Identifies the root cause of a connectivity fault from evidence
Writes a clear resolution with validation steps
modules.instructorNotes: Estimated time: 3 hours of lessons plus 1 hour of lab. Learners with networking experience can test out by attempting the lab first.

lessons.title: Layer models and encapsulation for security work
objectives: Map protocols and security controls to OSI and TCP/IP layers
Describe how encapsulation wraps a request in headers
Use the layer model to choose where to start troubleshooting

checks.question: A stateful firewall allows TCP 443 to a web server. At which layer does an SQL injection attack against that site happen, and can the firewall stop it?
options: Layer 7; no, the firewall only enforces addresses and ports
checks.explanation: Injection happens inside HTTP at the application layer. A control can only enforce what it can see.

checks.question: As a packet crosses two routers on its way to a server, which header normally changes at each hop?
checks.explanation: Layer 2 only describes the next link, so it is rebuilt at every hop. IP addresses stay the same unless NAT rewrites them.

checks.question: Which devices or controls inspect layer 7 content? Select all that apply.
checks.explanation: WAFs and application-aware firewalls read application data; switches and plain routers work at layers 2 and 3.

lessons.title: IP addressing, subnetting and CIDR
objectives: Calculate the network, broadcast and host range of an IPv4 prefix
Decide whether two hosts are on the same subnet
Recognise private, link-local and documentation addresses, and key IPv6 differences

checks.question: What is the network address of 10.40.9.77/22?
checks.explanation: /22 leaves 6 network bits in the third octet: block size 4, so 9 falls in the block starting at 8.

checks.question: How many usable host addresses does a /26 provide?
checks.explanation: 6 host bits = 64 addresses, minus the network and broadcast addresses.

checks.question: A laptop shows the address 169.254.20.11. What is the most likely explanation?
options: It is on the guest network
It failed to get an address from DHCP and assigned itself a link-local address
checks.explanation: 169.254.0.0/16 is link-local; Windows and macOS use it when DHCP does not answer.

checks.question: Which statements about IPv6 are true? Select all that apply.
options: Interfaces have link-local addresses even if nobody configured IPv6
NAT is required for IPv6 hosts to be secure
Firewalls and monitoring must cover IPv6 as well as IPv4
checks.explanation: IPv6 is often active by default. Filtering, not NAT, provides protection.

lessons.title: Switching, ARP and routing
objectives: Explain how switches, VLANs and ARP deliver traffic inside a subnet
Predict a host's next hop from its address, mask and gateway
Apply longest-prefix matching to a routing table
Identify the trust assumptions attackers abuse at layers 2 and 3

checks.question: Why can ARP be abused to intercept traffic on a LAN?
options: ARP is encrypted with a weak cipher
ARP replies are not authenticated, so any device can claim to own an IP address
checks.explanation: Hosts believe any ARP reply, which enables ARP spoofing and man-in-the-middle attacks.

checks.question: A router has routes for 10.0.0.0/8 (VPN), 10.10.0.0/16 (data-centre link) and 0.0.0.0/0 (internet). Which route is used for 10.10.0.15?
checks.explanation: The longest (most specific) matching prefix wins.

checks.question: A host is 10.40.9.77 with mask 255.255.255.0. Where does it send a packet for 10.40.10.5?
options: Directly, after an ARP request for 10.40.10.5
Nowhere: it is the broadcast address
checks.explanation: With a /24 mask, 10.40.10.5 is not on the host's subnet, so it goes to the gateway (even though on a /22 it would be local).

lessons.title: TCP, UDP and ports
objectives: Describe the TCP handshake, key flags and connection states
Interpret open, closed and filtered port responses
Explain why UDP is easy to spoof and abuse
Spot unusual ports and connection patterns in host and log output

checks.question: A scanner sends a SYN to TCP 3389 and receives an RST. What does that mean?
options: The port is closed but the host is reachable
A firewall silently dropped the packet
checks.explanation: SYN-ACK means open, RST means closed, silence usually means filtered.

checks.question: Why are UDP services used in reflection and amplification denial-of-service attacks?
options: UDP has no handshake, so the source address can be spoofed and replies sent to a victim
checks.explanation: Without a handshake, a spoofed request sends the (often larger) reply to the victim.

checks.question: A laptop shows SYN-SENT to 198.51.100.200:4444. Why is that worth investigating?
options: An outbound attempt to an unusual port with no business purpose can indicate malware
checks.explanation: Unusual outbound ports are classic signs of command-and-control or tooling; egress filtering should log them.

lessons.title: DHCP, DNS, NAT and TLS: the services behind every connection
objectives: Explain what DHCP, DNS, NAT/PAT and TLS each contribute to a connection
Identify how each service can be abused
Name the logs each service produces and what they prove

checks.question: A website reports abuse from Kanem's single public address at 14:02. What do you need to identify the internal host?
options: The edge firewall's NAT/PAT translation logs for 14:02
checks.explanation: With PAT, many hosts share one public address; only the translation logs map it back to an internal host and port.

checks.question: A rogue DHCP server appears on the staff network. What can it do? Select all that apply.
options: Give hosts a malicious default gateway
Give hosts a malicious DNS server
Read traffic already encrypted with TLS
Cause IP address conflicts and outages
checks.explanation: DHCP controls gateway and DNS settings, which can redirect traffic. It cannot decrypt TLS by itself.

checks.question: What can a network sensor normally still see about a TLS 1.3 connection without decrypting it?
options: The HTTP URLs and form data
IP addresses, ports, timing, volume, and usually the server name (SNI)
checks.explanation: TLS hides content but not metadata. Encrypted Client Hello can also hide the server name.

modules.title: Network Threats and Attack Surfaces
modules.purpose:
Defenders need to know what they are defending against. This module covers the main network threats from the defender's side: reconnaissance and scanning, spoofing and interception, denial of service, credential attacks and lateral movement, and command and control. For each one you learn what is at risk, the signs it leaves and the controls that prevent or limit it. You finish by matching threats to their signs and controls for Kanem and prioritising the fixes.

**To complete this module:** finish all five lessons and pass the lab (80%), including the written threat summary.
objectives: Describe the main network threats and what they put at risk
Recognise the signs each threat leaves in logs and monitoring
Choose preventive and detective controls for each threat
Use MITRE ATT&CK to name and look up behaviours
Prioritise controls for an organisation
keyConcepts: Volumetric, state and application denial of service
modules.instructorNotes: Estimated time: 2.5 hours of lessons plus 1 hour of lab. Threats are taught from the defender's side only: risks, signs and controls.

lessons.title: Reconnaissance and scanning
objectives: Distinguish passive and active reconnaissance
Recognise scanning in firewall and IDS logs
Reduce what reconnaissance can learn

checks.question: Which kind of reconnaissance leaves no trace in your own logs?
options: Searching public sources such as DNS records and job adverts
checks.explanation: Passive reconnaissance never touches your network.

checks.question: An internal host suddenly tries many ports on many servers. What is the right first step?
options: Check whether an authorised scanner or change ticket explains it
checks.explanation: Authorised scanning looks the same; context decides.

checks.question: Which reduce what reconnaissance can learn? Select all that apply.
options: Exposing only the services that are needed
Removing old DNS records and version banners
checks.explanation: Less exposed means less to learn.

lessons.title: Spoofing and interception
objectives: Explain why some protocols can be impersonated
Recognise signs of spoofing
Choose controls that prevent or limit it

checks.question: Which control protects traffic even if it is redirected?
checks.explanation: Encryption with certificate checking is the backstop.

checks.question: Which switch features block false DHCP servers and forged address-resolution replies?
options: DHCP snooping and dynamic ARP inspection
checks.explanation: Both rely on the table of trusted address assignments.

checks.question: Which suggest spoofing? Select all that apply.
options: The gateway's hardware address suddenly changes
A familiar Wi-Fi name from an unknown access point
checks.explanation: Each points to impersonation.

lessons.title: Denial of service
objectives: Distinguish volumetric, state-exhaustion and application-layer denial of service
Tell an attack from a legitimate surge
Prepare protection and a response runbook

checks.question: Why must protection against very large floods sit upstream of your internet link?
options: Once the link is full, nothing behind it can help
checks.explanation: Scrubbing happens before traffic reaches you.

checks.question: Salary day doubles traffic to the portal. How do you avoid mistaking it for an attack?
options: Compare with baselines and a calendar of business events
Assume every surge is an attack
checks.explanation: Know what normal peaks look like.

checks.question: Which help against application-layer floods? Select all that apply.
options: A CDN and web application firewall
Rate limits on logins and expensive pages
checks.explanation: Absorb, filter and limit.

lessons.title: Credential attacks and lateral movement
objectives: Recognise credential misuse in authentication logs
Recognise unusual movement between systems
Reduce both with MFA, segmentation and privilege controls

checks.question: Failed sign-ins spread across many accounts from one source, a few each, suggest what?
checks.explanation: Few attempts per account avoid lockouts.

checks.question: Which control most reduces the value of a stolen password?
checks.explanation: A password alone is then not enough.

checks.question: Which limit how far an intruder can move from one compromised machine? Select all that apply.
options: Administration only from a management zone through a jump host
One shared admin password for every server
checks.explanation: A shared password lets one capture open everything.

lessons.title: Command and control
objectives: Explain why malicious software needs to communicate out
Recognise behavioural signs in outbound traffic
Use egress controls and detections to make it harder and more visible

checks.question: Why is outbound traffic a good place to find an intrusion?
options: Malicious software usually has to talk out to its operator
checks.explanation: Watch the exits.

checks.question: Which control forces outbound traffic through points you monitor?
options: Egress filtering with proxies and internal resolvers
checks.explanation: Default-deny outbound, through watched routes.

checks.question: Which together justify escalating a laptop? Select all that apply.
options: A destination domain first seen three days ago
Traffic bypassing the proxy at night
Reading the company intranet at lunch
checks.explanation: Several signs on one host.

modules.title: Firewalls and Network Access Control
modules.purpose:
An auditor has found that Kanem Financial Services' head-office firewall has not been reviewed in five years. In this module you learn how firewalls make decisions, how rule sets drift, how to rebuild a policy on least privilege, how to run firewall changes safely, and how network access control keeps unknown devices out. You finish by reviewing and redesigning the real-looking policy yourself.

**To complete this module:** finish all five lessons and pass the lab (80%), including the written change request.
modules.prerequisiteKnowledge: IP addressing, TCP/UDP ports and the client–server model (module 1). Basic familiarity with network diagrams.
objectives: Analyse an ordered rule set and predict how it decides a connection
Identify shadowed, redundant, over-general and unlogged rules
Design a least-privilege policy, including egress filtering, from business requirements
Document a firewall change with justification, testing and rollback
Recommend network access control methods for managed, legacy and guest devices
assessmentCriteria: Correctly identifies excessive and shadowed rules in a rule set
Builds a rule set that passes all test connections
Produces a change request with testing and rollback
Explains the risk of each finding in business terms
modules.instructorNotes: Estimated time: 2.5 hours of lessons plus 1.5 hours of lab. The lab's night-time DMZ SSH traffic is a deliberate seed for the module 9 incident.

lessons.title: How firewalls decide: stateless, stateful and application-aware
objectives: Compare stateless, stateful and application-aware filtering
Explain what a stateful firewall can and cannot protect against
Choose the right firewall type for a given boundary

checks.question: A router ACL allows users to reach a web server on TCP 443. Users report the page never loads. The ACL has no other rules. What is the most likely cause?
options: The ACL is stateless, so the return traffic from the server is not allowed
TCP 443 needs TLS inspection to work
checks.explanation: Stateless filters judge each packet alone, so replies need their own rule. A stateful firewall would allow the replies automatically.
optionFeedback: Possible in general, but the question points at the filter design.
Right: no rule allows server → user packets back to the ephemeral port.
TLS inspection is optional and unrelated to basic connectivity.
ACLs filter on TCP ports all the time.

checks.question: Which threats does a stateful firewall that allows internet → dmz TCP 443 NOT stop? Select all that apply.
options: An injection attack against the web application on port 443
A forged "reply" packet that matches no existing connection
A connection attempt from the internet to the DMZ on TCP 22
Malware on the web server downloading a tool over HTTPS if outbound 443 is allowed
checks.explanation: Stateful inspection tracks conversations, not content. Traffic on an allowed port, inbound or outbound, passes. Unmatched replies and non-allowed ports are blocked.

checks.question: Which control is designed to inspect the content of HTTP requests for attacks such as injection?
checks.explanation: A WAF understands HTTP requests and their parameters. Network firewalls decide on addresses, ports, applications and users.

lessons.title: Rule order, shadowing and default deny
objectives: Predict the result of a connection against an ordered rule set
Identify shadowed, redundant and over-general rules
Justify an explicit, logged default deny

checks.question: Using first-match evaluation, what happens to a connection from users to servers on TCP 3389?
checks.code:
1  ALLOW  users  any      tcp 3389
2  DENY   any    servers  tcp 3389
3  DENY   any    any      any any
checks.explanation: Rule 1 matches first (destination "any" includes servers), so the connection is allowed. Rules 1 and 2 overlap with different actions, a correlation problem.

checks.question: A deny rule has had zero hits in 90 days and sits below a broad allow rule for the same zone pair. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The rule is shadowed by the broad allow above it
checks.explanation: Zero hits is consistent with shadowing: the earlier allow matches the traffic first. Confirm by checking whether the allow covers every field of the deny.

checks.question: Why make the default deny explicit and logged, even when the firewall has an implicit deny?
options: It records blocked attempts (scans, malware, misconfigurations) and makes the policy obvious to reviewers
Implicit denies do not work on stateful firewalls
checks.explanation: The explicit, logged deny turns blocked traffic into evidence and documents the policy. It is good practice rather than a hard rule in standards.

lessons.title: Least privilege, inbound and egress filtering
objectives: Translate business requirements into least-privilege rules
Explain why egress filtering limits command-and-control and exfiltration
Correct rules written in the wrong direction or with excessive scope

checks.question: IT support must take remote control of staff laptops with RDP. Which rule is least privilege?
checks.explanation: Support connects from the management zone to users, on RDP only. The other rules are in the wrong direction or far too broad.
optionFeedback: Wrong direction, and lets every laptop RDP to every server and the internet.
Lets guest, DMZ and internet sources reach laptop RDP.
Right: one source zone, one destination zone, one service.

checks.question: Which outbound rules give an attacker on a compromised server the easiest path to steal data? Select all that apply.
checks.explanation: Unrestricted outbound access from servers allows command-and-control and exfiltration on any port. DNS to internal resolvers and patching through a proxy are narrow and monitored.

checks.question: A rule reads "ALLOW any → dmz any any — temp vendor access INC-2291 (Nov 2025)". It is now March 2026. What is the main issue?
options: The ticket number is in the wrong format
A temporary, all-ports rule from the internet into the DMZ was never removed
DMZ rules should be at the bottom
checks.explanation: Temporary rules need an expiry, an owner and a check that they were removed. This one exposes every port on every DMZ host.

lessons.title: Firewall logging, rule review and change management
objectives: Select the firewall events that must be logged
Review a rule set against usage, ownership and design
Write a firewall change request with testing and rollback

checks.question: Put these change steps in a sensible order for retiring a broad rule that has many hits: (A) disable the broad rule with logging on, (B) analyse logs to see what legitimately uses it, (C) remove the broad rule after the agreed period, (D) add narrow rules for the legitimate traffic above it.
checks.explanation: Understand the traffic, add the narrow replacements, disable the broad rule while watching for breakage, then remove it.

checks.question: Which events should be logged on a perimeter firewall? Select all that apply.
options: Connections denied by the default rule
Administrator logins and rule changes on the firewall
Allowed connections into the server and management zones
Every packet of every allowed web-browsing session
checks.explanation: Denies, administrative actions and allows across sensitive boundaries are the most valuable. Per-packet logging of normal browsing adds cost and noise; connection-level logs are enough.

checks.question: In a rule review, an allow rule has an owner and ticket but zero hits for 180 days. What is the best action?
options: Keep it, because it has an owner
Confirm with the owner whether it is still needed; if not, remove it through change control
Convert it to a deny rule
checks.explanation: An unused allow rule is pure risk, but confirm before removing: some flows are seasonal (year-end jobs). Removal still goes through change control.

lessons.title: Network access control: who gets on the network
objectives: Describe the 802.1X supplicant, authenticator and authentication server roles
Choose suitable access methods for managed devices, legacy devices and guests
Position NAC alongside firewalls and zero trust

checks.question: In 802.1X, which component keeps the switch port closed until authentication succeeds?
checks.explanation: The authenticator (switch or access point) controls the port. The supplicant is the client; the authentication server (usually RADIUS) makes the decision.

checks.question: A building has CCTV cameras that cannot run an 802.1X supplicant. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Disable NAC for the whole switch
Use MAC authentication bypass and place the cameras in a restricted segment that only reaches the video recorder
Put the cameras in the users VLAN
Give the cameras the Wi-Fi password
checks.explanation: MAB is the usual fallback, but MAC addresses are easy to copy, so the segment must be tightly restricted and monitored.

checks.question: Why is EAP-TLS generally considered stronger than password-based 802.1X methods?
options: Each device proves its identity with a certificate, so there is no password to phish or guess and devices can be revoked individually
It does not need a RADIUS server
checks.explanation: Certificate-based authentication removes shared or user passwords from the network login. It needs a certificate infrastructure to manage.

modules.title: Network Segmentation and Zero Trust
modules.purpose:
Kanem's Lagos data centre runs everything in one flat server network, and the CIO wants a design in which one compromised system cannot take the rest with it. This module covers zones, DMZs and trust boundaries; how VLANs and firewalls actually enforce segmentation; microsegmentation for east–west traffic; Zero Trust Architecture as described by NIST and CISA; and protecting and validating the management plane. You finish by designing and justifying the new segmentation.

**To complete this module:** finish all five lessons and pass the lab (80%), including the written rationale.
modules.prerequisiteKnowledge: Modules 1 and 3 (addressing, routing and firewall policy).
objectives: Design zones and trust boundaries for a data centre
Explain how VLANs, firewalls and host controls enforce segmentation
Plan microsegmentation for east–west traffic
Apply zero trust principles to remote, third-party and administrative access
Validate segmentation with recorded tests and evidence
assessmentCriteria: Builds a policy that passes all test flows
Makes zero trust and management-plane decisions correctly
Writes a justified design with a validation plan
modules.instructorNotes: Estimated time: 2.5 hours of lessons plus 1.5 hours of lab.

lessons.title: Zones, DMZs and trust boundaries
objectives: Group systems into zones by trust and function
Distinguish north–south from east–west traffic
Design DMZ rules that keep paths inward narrow

checks.question: The public website in the DMZ needs product data. Which design is best?
options: DMZ web server → database zone directly on 1433
DMZ web server → internal application API on one port; only the application tier reaches the database
Move the database into the DMZ
Allow the DMZ to reach the internal network on all ports
checks.explanation: A compromised DMZ host should reach as little as possible; one API call is far narrower than direct database access.

checks.question: Which traffic is east–west?
options: A customer reaching the public website
A staff laptop connecting to an internal application server
An email arriving from the internet
checks.explanation: East–west traffic stays inside the organisation and is the path of lateral movement.

checks.question: Why is a staff laptop usually less trusted than a database server, even though both are internal?
options: Laptops browse the web, open email and travel, so they are more exposed to compromise
checks.explanation: Trust should follow exposure and function, not physical location.

lessons.title: VLANs, subnets and where segmentation is enforced
objectives: Explain why a VLAN alone is not a security control
Align VLANs, subnets and zones
Apply switch hardening that keeps VLANs separate
Choose controls for east–west traffic inside a zone

checks.question: All VLANs route through a core switch with routing enabled and no ACLs. How segmented is the network?
options: Effectively flat: every VLAN can reach every other
Only the guest VLAN is isolated
checks.explanation: The routing device decides; without filtering, VLANs only separate broadcast domains.

checks.question: Which are sound switch hardening practices for keeping VLANs separate? Select all that apply.
options: Disable automatic trunk negotiation on access ports
Allow only the required VLANs on each trunk
checks.explanation: Explicit trunks, pruned VLAN lists and disabled ports reduce layer-2 leakage. VLAN 1 should not carry users.

checks.question: Ten database servers share one VLAN. What limits a compromised database from reaching the other nine?
options: Host-based firewalls or microsegmentation on each server
checks.explanation: Traffic inside a VLAN never reaches the zone firewall, so per-host controls are needed.

lessons.title: Microsegmentation
objectives: Explain how microsegmentation differs from zone segmentation
Compare host, hypervisor, cloud-native and identity-based enforcement
Plan a staged rollout that avoids outages

checks.question: What is the first step in a safe microsegmentation rollout?
options: Block everything and wait for complaints
Inventory and label workloads, then observe real traffic
checks.explanation: Policy must be built from known, legitimate flows; enforcing before observing causes outages.

checks.question: Microsegmentation rules are usually expressed in terms of:
options: Workload labels or identities (application, environment, role)
checks.explanation: Labels and identities follow the workload wherever it runs.

checks.question: Why enforce in monitoring mode before blocking?
options: To find undocumented dependencies by logging what would be blocked
checks.explanation: Logging would-be blocks reveals flows nobody documented before they cause an outage.

lessons.title: Zero Trust Architecture
objectives: Explain the zero trust tenets in NIST SP 800-207
Describe the policy engine, administrator and enforcement point
Plan a zero trust journey using the CISA maturity model
Redesign remote access on zero trust principles

checks.question: In NIST SP 800-207, which component makes the access decision?
checks.explanation: The policy engine decides; the administrator signals the enforcement point, which allows or blocks the session.

checks.question: Which statements reflect zero trust principles? Select all that apply.
options: Access is granted per session to specific resources
Being on the internal network is enough to be trusted
Decisions use identity, device health and context
Communication is secured regardless of network location
checks.explanation: Zero trust removes implicit trust based on location.

checks.question: A contractor needs the loans application for three months. Which approach best follows zero trust?
options: A full VPN account with access to the whole network
Application-level access with MFA, device checks, a time limit and logging
Open the application to the internet
checks.explanation: Give access to the one resource needed, decided per session, for a limited time.

lessons.title: Protecting the management plane and validating segmentation
objectives: Design controls for administrative access to infrastructure
Plan segmentation validation with test flows, configuration review and flow logs
Record test results as evidence with owners and retest dates

checks.question: Which controls belong in a protected management plane? Select all that apply.
options: Admin interfaces reachable only from the management zone
Jump hosts or privileged access workstations
Named admin accounts with MFA and central logging
checks.explanation: Telnet sends credentials in clear text; secure protocols only.

checks.question: A segmentation test finds that the DMZ can still reach the database on 1433 through a "temp migration" rule. What should happen?
options: Record a finding with an owner and ticket, remove or narrow the rule, and retest
Move the database into the DMZ
checks.explanation: Each failed test becomes a tracked finding with remediation and retesting.

checks.question: Why compare flow logs with the segmentation design?
options: Traffic on paths that should be closed reveals misconfigurations or unknown dependencies
checks.explanation: Observed traffic is evidence of what the network actually allows.

modules.title: IDS, IPS and Network Detection
modules.purpose:
Detection tools only help if their alerts are trusted. This module covers how network detection works, alert quality, sensor placement and telemetry, triage and tuning, and the limits that encryption and prevention impose. You finish by triaging a night of alerts and writing a tuning plan.

**To complete this module:** finish all five lessons and pass the lab (80%), including the written tuning plan.
objectives: Explain detection methods, IDS versus IPS, and alert contents
Measure alert quality and coverage
Place sensors and collect telemetry
Triage alerts with context
Tune detections without creating blind spots
Explain encrypted-traffic limits and TLS inspection trade-offs
keyConcepts: True and false positives and negatives
modules.instructorNotes: Estimated time: 2.5 hours of lessons plus 1 hour of lab. Lessons name Suricata and Zeek as example open-source tools; the concepts apply to commercial products.

lessons.title: How network detection works
objectives: Compare signature, anomaly and stateful protocol analysis
Explain IDS versus IPS and network versus host detection
Read what an alert contains

checks.question: Which detection method is most precise for known threats but misses new ones?
checks.explanation: Signatures match known patterns.

checks.question: What is the main extra risk of running a system inline as an IPS?
options: A wrong block stops legitimate traffic, and the device can become a bottleneck or single point of failure
It only works in the cloud
checks.explanation: Prevention needs well-tuned rules and resilience.

checks.question: Which details does a useful alert include? Select all that apply.
options: Time and the rule that fired
Source and destination addresses and ports
checks.explanation: Enough to start triage.

lessons.title: Alert quality: true and false positives
objectives: Use the four outcomes: TP, FP, TN, FN
Explain why most alerts are noise
Measure detections by volume, true-positive rate, coverage and time to triage

checks.question: Which outcome is the most dangerous?
checks.explanation: A missed attack leaves no alert at all.

checks.question: How do you measure coverage?
options: Map detections to the attacker behaviours (ATT&CK techniques) they can see
checks.explanation: Coverage is about what you can detect at all.

checks.question: A rule produces 300 alerts a day and almost none are worth investigating. What is the effect?
options: Analysts lose trust in the rule and may miss the real one
checks.explanation: Noise hides signal.

lessons.title: Sensor placement and telemetry
objectives: Choose how traffic reaches a sensor
Place sensors where they see what matters
Collect telemetry beyond alerts and keep time and context consistent

checks.question: Which way of feeding a sensor is most reliable and complete?
options: A switch mirror port under heavy load
checks.explanation: Mirror ports can drop copies under load.

checks.question: Which placement sees movement between internal zones towards critical systems?
checks.explanation: East-west traffic needs internal sensors.

checks.question: Which telemetry helps triage beyond alerts? Select all that apply.
checks.explanation: Context comes from many sources.

lessons.title: Triage and tuning
objectives: Apply a five-step triage routine
Tell true positives, benign true positives and false positives apart
Tune with scoped exceptions, thresholds and enrichment without creating blind spots

checks.question: The vulnerability scanner triggers a port-scan rule during its scheduled window. What is the best tuning?
options: A scoped exception for that source, rule and time window
checks.explanation: Scope the exception narrowly.

checks.question: The same rule fires for an unknown VPN address with no change ticket. What is it most likely to be?
options: A possible true positive to investigate and escalate
checks.explanation: Only context separates the two.

content.scenario: You have joined the security team at **Kanem Financial Services** (fictional). The internal auditor has asked for a review of **FW-HQ-01**, the stateful firewall between the six head-office zones (see the network diagram in lesson 3). content.instructions:
1. Read **Current policy** and **Rule 4 traffic summary**.
2. Answer tasks 1–6 (the review).
3. Build the replacement policy in task 7 from **Connectivity requirements**. The grader tests it against 22 connections it does not show you; all must behave as required.

documents.title: Connectivity requirements (approved by the CIO)
documents.body:
1. Anyone on the **internet** may reach the public website in the **dmz** on TCP 443.
2. **users** may browse the **internet** on TCP 443.
3. **users** may reach the core banking application in **servers** on TCP 443.
4. The **dmz** web server may reach the database in **servers** on TCP 5432 and nothing else.
5. **management** may administer **servers** and the **dmz** over SSH (TCP 22).
6. IT support in **management** may take remote control of **users** laptops over RDP (TCP 3389).
7. **servers** may reach the **internet** for DNS (UDP 53) and patch downloads (TCP 443).
8. **guest** Wi-Fi may reach the **internet** on TCP 80 and 443 only.
9. No other zone may connect into **management**.
10. Everything else must be blocked.

*In production, server patching and DNS would go through a proxy and internal resolvers, and rules would name hosts rather than whole zones. The simulator works with zones to keep the exercise focused.*

validator.debrief:
## Worked solution

**Excessive rules: 2, 4, 7, 8, 10 and 11.** Rule 2 exposes every port on every DMZ host to the internet (and other zones); rule 4 lets a compromised web server reach every TCP port on every server; rule 7 lets every laptop open RDP to every server and the internet (lateral movement, ATT&CK T1021.001); rule 8 lets servers send anything anywhere (command-and-control and exfiltration); rule 10 lets an untrusted guest network reach internal servers; rule 11 exposes the firewall administration console to the users zone. Rules 1, 3, 5 and 9 match approved needs.

**Shadowed: rule 6.** Rule 4 (dmz → servers, any TCP port) matches DMZ SSH first, so rule 6 never fires: zero hits confirms it. The DMZ SSH connection in task 3 is therefore **allowed by rule 4**.

**Rule 12** is a correct default deny, but with logging off it destroys the evidence of scans and blocked outbound attempts.

**Rule 4 replacement:** a single logged rule for the web server to the loans database on TCP 5432. The SMB and night-time SSH traffic from the web server is not business traffic: treat it as a possible compromise, preserve logs and escalate before the change, not after.

### A rule set that passes

```text
#   Action  Source      Destination  Proto  Port
1   ALLOW   internet    dmz          tcp    443
2   ALLOW   users       internet     tcp    443
3   ALLOW   users       servers      tcp    443
4   ALLOW   dmz         servers      tcp    5432
5   ALLOW   management  servers      tcp    22
6   ALLOW   management  dmz          tcp    22
7   ALLOW   management  users        tcp    3389
8   ALLOW   servers     internet     udp    53
9   ALLOW   servers     internet     tcp    443
10  ALLOW   guest       internet     tcp    80
11  ALLOW   guest       internet     tcp    443
    (implicit deny for everything else; log it)
```

Order matters less here because no rule overlaps another, which is itself a sign of a clean design.

### What a strong change request includes

The rules affected with before/after definitions; why now (audit finding, exposure of the DMZ and servers); impact and timing (an agreed low-traffic window, digital channels and IT support informed); testing (run each required connection, watch hit counters on the new rules and the deny log for 7 days); rollback (re-enable the old rules from the saved configuration within 15 minutes); and approval by the change board and the rule owners.

## What you have practised

This is the work of a firewall or network security review in a real organisation: reading a rule set the way the device does, connecting each finding to a concrete attack path, rebuilding the policy from approved requirements and planning the change so the business keeps running. It maps to NIST SP 800-53 SC-7 and CM-3 and CIS Controls 12 and 13.

**Next:** module 4 replaces zone-wide rules with real segmentation and identity-aware access.

validator.debrief:
## Worked solution

**Root cause:** LN-PC-14 was set up manually (DHCP disabled) by the contractor with gateway **10.40.9.1**, which does not exist, and mask **255.255.255.0** instead of /22. The printer at 10.40.9.30 is inside the laptop's /24, so the laptop reaches it directly with ARP: that is why "printer works". Everything off its subnet, including the DNS server and core banking, goes to 10.40.9.1, which never answers ARP, so Windows reports *Destination host unreachable* from the laptop itself.

**Fix:** re-enable DHCP so the laptop receives 10.40.9.77/22 (or a new lease), gateway 10.40.8.1 and DNS 10.10.0.53.

**Validate:** `ipconfig` shows DHCP enabled, mask 255.255.252.0 and gateway 10.40.8.1; `ping 10.40.8.1` replies; `nslookup corebanking.kanem.example` returns 10.10.0.15; `tracert -d 10.10.0.15` goes 10.40.8.1 → 172.31.0.1 → … → 10.10.0.15; the user opens the app.

**Separate issue:** the copier at 10.40.12.40 saturating the internet link explains "internet is slow" but not this failure (the VPN is prioritised). Raise it with the branch: schedule large uploads out of hours or rate-limit them.

**Advanced challenge:** with a /24 mask, any staff address outside 10.40.9.0/24 (for example 10.40.10.5) looks remote, so the laptop sends it to the router, which forwards it straight back into VLAN 20. It works, but it adds a hop and load on the router.

### Sequence
1 ARP for the gateway → 2 DNS query → 3 TCP SYN → 4 router forwards over the VPN (10.0.0.0/8 is more specific than the default route) → 5 TLS handshake.

## What you have practised

Structured troubleshooting by layer, subnet arithmetic, host forwarding decisions and longest-prefix routing: the foundation for reading firewall rules, segmentation designs and incident evidence in the rest of the course. Keeping the bandwidth symptom separate from the root cause is exactly the discipline incident responders need.

**Next:** module 2 uses the same packet-level thinking to recognise attacks.

## Worked solution

**Placement:** WEB-01 → dmz; CORE-APP → app; CORE-DB → db; CARD-SW → cards; JUMP-01 → mgmt; laptops → users; visitor Wi-Fi → guest.

### A policy that passes

```text

1   ALLOW   internet  dmz          tcp    443
2   ALLOW   dmz       app          tcp    8443
3   ALLOW   users     app          tcp    443
4   ALLOW   app       db           tcp    1433
5   ALLOW   app       cards        tcp    9443
6   ALLOW   cards     internet     tcp    443
7   ALLOW   mgmt      dmz          tcp    22
8   ALLOW   mgmt      app          tcp    22
9   ALLOW   mgmt      db           tcp    22
10  ALLOW   mgmt      cards        tcp    22
11  ALLOW   users     internet     tcp    443
12  ALLOW   guest     internet     tcp    443
    (everything else denied and logged)
```

**Requests:** A, application-level access with MFA, device checks, an end date and logging (zero trust); B, refuse, administration only through JUMP-01; C, allow only the specific cluster or replication flows, enforced per host.

### What a strong rationale covers

Zones follow exposure and data: the DMZ is internet-facing and may only call the application API, never the databases, so a compromised website cannot read customer data directly. Cards is separate because it is the highest-value system and needs the smallest set of flows. Nothing connects into mgmt, and administration happens only from JUMP-01 with MFA. Application, database and card systems cannot start internet connections except the card processor flow, which limits command-and-control and exfiltration. Inside zones, host firewalls or microsegmentation limit east–west traffic. Contractors get application-level, time-limited access instead of a VPN. Validation: an expected-allow test for each approved flow and expected-deny tests from every other zone, firewall configuration review, and a check of flow logs for traffic on closed paths, repeated after major changes and at least annually.

## What you have practised

This is network security architecture: turning a business requirement ("one compromise must not take the rest") into zones, boundaries, policy, access decisions and a validation plan, and documenting why. It reflects NIST SP 800-207 and the CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model.

**Next:** module 5 adds detection: what you do when an attacker moves anyway.

## Worked solution

**Device:** KAN-LT-118. KAN-LT-077 held 10.40.9.44 until 01:00; KAN-LT-118 took it at 01:12. Using the IP alone would have blamed the wrong laptop.

**Indicators for 10.40.9.44:** long random-looking subdomains with TXT lookups to one domain, a 60-second rhythm, a domain registered three days ago and never seen before, and about 200 times the normal outbound DNS volume. There was no NXDOMAIN burst and no external resolver use.

**DHCP:** a device on Gi1/0/23 answered DHCP with its own gateway. Remove it and enable DHCP snooping with only the uplink trusted.

**Encrypted DNS:** manage browsers and devices to use Kanem's resolvers; block or alert on direct DNS, DoT and DoH to outside resolvers.

**Email:** DMARC p=none only monitors. Fix the payroll sender first, then move to quarantine and later reject while watching the reports.

**A model escalation:** "Since 01:20 UTC on 10 March, KAN-LT-118 (user a.musa, Finance; IP 10.40.9.44 per the DHCP lease from 01:12) has made 4,210 TXT lookups for long random-looking subdomains of k7q-sync.example every 60 seconds. The domain was registered three days ago and has not been seen at Kanem before. Overnight DNS volume was about 9 MB, roughly 200 times normal. An endpoint alert (suspicious script from an email attachment) fired at 01:18 and has not been reviewed. Checked: DHCP lease, resolver logs, proxy and endpoint console. Not checked: email gateway, file access, other hosts querying the domain. Recommend: incident lead to approve isolating KAN-LT-118, blocking k7q-sync.example at the resolvers, and searching for other hosts that queried it."

## What you have practised

Joining DHCP, DNS, proxy and endpoint evidence into a decision, and fixing the configuration gaps that make investigations harder: core skills for network security and SOC roles.

validator.debrief:
## Worked solution

**RTT:** frame 3 (0.002600) to frame 4 (0.040600) = **38 ms**, normal for the Abuja–Lagos WAN.

**TLS:** the Client Hello (frame 6) carries SNI **portal.kanem.example** and offers TLS 1.3 and 1.2; the Server Hello (frame 7) selects **TLS 1.3** (0x0304) in supported_versions, although the record header says 0x0303.

**Loss:** frame 11 arrives with a gap ("previous segment not captured"); the client sends three duplicate ACKs (frames 12, 14, 16) and the server fast-retransmits the missing 1,400 bytes in frame 17, about 39 ms later. One lost segment, recovered quickly: worth watching, not the cause.

**Unanswered server:** `static.kanem.example` resolves to **10.10.0.16** (frames 19–20). The client's SYN to 10.10.0.16:443 (frame 21) is retransmitted **3 times** (frames 22–24, at about +1, +3 and +7 s) with no SYN-ACK or RST. Filter: `tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0`.

**Cause:** the page waits more than 7 seconds for its images, scripts and styles from the server migrated in CHG-3318. Silence (no RST) suggests traffic is being **dropped**, most likely by a firewall rule or a missing route for the new address. Confidence: medium; confirm with the firewall logs.

**Limitations:** one capture point (the laptop); content is encrypted; the capture cannot show where the SYNs are dropped.

**Recommendations:** check firewall policy and routing from the Abuja staff zone (10.40.8.0/22) to 10.10.0.16:443; capture on the server side to confirm whether SYNs arrive; add a post-migration connectivity test to the change process; keep watching for loss on the WAN.

## What you have practised

Measuring, reading and explaining real protocol behaviour, then reporting it so others can repeat it: core skills for network engineers and analysts.

**Next:** module 9 brings these skills into network incident response.

**Timeline (UTC, Saturday 14 March 2026)**

IdsAlerts
| where SrcIP == "10.30.0.40" or DstIP == "10.30.0.40"
| distinct Signature

FlowRecords
| where SrcIP == "10.30.0.40"
| summarize Received = sum(BytesToSrc) by DstIP, DstPort

| summarize Out = sum(BytesToSrc)

**Root cause:** rule 2 (temporary vendor access since November 2025) exposed SSH with password login on dmz-vendor-01 to the internet; rule 4 let the DMZ reach every TCP port in the server zone. Both had logging off, so the firewall recorded nothing; flows were the only network evidence. The data was pulled from the file server and sent out through the intruder's own SSH session, which a stateful firewall treats as return traffic.

**Severity:** critical. Finance and customer loan files were likely taken; brief the DPO and legal.

**Containment:** export evidence; isolate dmz-vendor-01 without powering off and capture memory and disk; disable rule 2; restrict rule 4 to 10.30.0.10 → 10.10.0.22:1433 with logging; block both addresses and the domain; reset credentials; check file-srv-01.

**Recommendations:** retire temporary rules on their end date (module 3); log every allow rule crossing a boundary; key-based SSH only, and never internet-facing for support boxes; correlation rules for DMZ-to-server-zone connections and for large outbound volumes; quarterly rule reviews.

## Worked solution (one good answer; others are possible)

**Weaknesses:** rules 2 and 4 (the path in INC-2318), the flat servers zone, user access to management and RDP everywhere, unlogged allow rules, single firewall and link, broad VPN and weak vendor access. WPA3-Enterprise, modern TLS and the SIEM are strengths.

**Target zones**

| Zone | Contents | Reached from |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DMZ | Public website | Internet on 443 only |
| Application servers | Core banking app, other app servers, patch server | Users on 443 to the app; DMZ only to the new rates API |
| Restricted | Core banking database, finance file server | Application servers on named ports only |
| Management | Jump host, admin workstations | IT staff via MFA; device management only from here |
| Users | Staff laptops | Internet via proxy; app servers on 443 |
| Kiosk | Lobby kiosk | One published calculator endpoint only |
| Guest | Visitors | Internet only |
| (none) | Vendors and remote staff | ZTNA to named applications, time-limited for vendors |

**Flows:** F1, F2 and F6 allowed on named ports and logged; F3 only via the jump host with MFA; F4 through ZTNA; F5 redesigned as a read-only rates API (the DMZ never reaches the database); F7 through the patch server or egress proxy.

**Policy statements:** default deny at every boundary; every boundary allow rule logs; every rule has an owner, purpose and review date (temporary rules expire automatically); quarterly rule review; changes through change control with rollback; devices hardened to CIS benchmarks with central MFA authentication.

**Monitoring plan:** SIEM detections for any connection into the restricted zone from outside the application servers, any DMZ connection to internal zones other than the rates API, large outbound volumes, management access not from the jump host, and logging changes on firewalls.

**Roadmap:** *Now:* remove rule 2; restrict rules 4, 7, 10 and 11; log every boundary rule; retire dmz-vendor-01 and move the vendor to ZTNA. *Next:* HA firewall pair and second link; split servers into application and restricted zones; ZTNA for remote staff. *Later (year two):* NAC and microsegmentation of the restricted zone.

**Validation:** approved tests under rules of engagement: guest reaches nothing internal; the DMZ reaches only the rates API; the users zone cannot reach management except via the jump host; every boundary rule produces SIEM logs; firewall failover completes within the agreed time; an independent penetration test of the DMZ and restricted zone.

**CSF 2.0:** Govern (policy, owners, acceptances), Identify (asset and flow inventory, register), Protect (zones, rules, ZTNA, hardening), Detect (logging and detections), Respond (module 9 playbooks), Recover (HA, configuration backups, tested failover).

The whole job of a network security architect: turning evidence and requirements into a defensible design, a funded plan and tests that prove it. Keep these deliverables for your portfolio.

**Triage:** scanner, benign true positive (CHG-310); large ICMP, false positive for the monitoring server's MTU checks; printers, a real policy issue already being fixed (CHG-334); SQL keywords, real but failed probes (404/403); new domain, benign (verified partner); **10.20.6.31, true positive: escalate**. A Finance user on an unmanaged device reached four restricted servers over SMB and swept the server zone at 03:12–03:14, with no ticket.

**Tuning that cuts noise without blind spots:**

| Change | Scope | Owner / review |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scanner exception | Source 10.99.0.20, port-sweep rule only, 01:30–03:30, CHG-310 | SOC lead, review quarterly |
| Monitoring exception | Source 10.99.0.12, large-ICMP rule only | SOC lead, quarterly |
| Printer TLS to informational | 10.20.9.200–210 until CHG-334 closes | Network team, April |
| SQL keywords | High only when the response is 200 or 500 | Detection engineer |
| Enrichment | Raise severity for restricted core servers as destination | Detection engineer |

Expected effect: about 160 fewer alerts a night (the scanner and monitoring exceptions), with the printers downgraded and the 10.20.6.31 alerts still firing.

**Gap:** no sensor after the VPN concentrator or between the core banking tiers; add one (or flow telemetry) there.

**Testing tuning:** replay tonight's alerts and known-bad examples against the new rules; confirm that a sweep from any address other than 10.99.0.20 still alerts.

## What you have practised

The daily detection work of a SOC: triage with context, scoped tuning and measuring what you can see.

validator.debrief:
## Worked solution

| Threat | Typical sign | Best control | ATT&CK | Kanem gap |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Reconnaissance | Many attempts to many ports or hosts | Expose only needed services; default deny | T1595 | Few: keep exposure low |
| Spoofing | Gateway address changes, certificate warnings | TLS with validation; DHCP snooping and ARP inspection | T1557 | No switch protections; staff click through warnings |
| Denial of service | Capacity exhausted with no business reason | Upstream scrubbing, CDN, rate limits | T1498 | No protection, one provider |
| Password spraying | Failures across many accounts from one source | Phishing-resistant MFA, no exemptions | T1110.003 | 35 exempt accounts; no alert |
| Lateral movement | Accounts reaching many systems over admin protocols | Segmentation, jump host, unique local passwords | T1021 | RDP from users to anything; shared admin password |
| Command and control | Regular outbound connections to rare destinations | Egress filtering through proxies and resolvers | TA0011 | Direct HTTPS and DNS allowed |

**Preventive:** MFA, DHCP snooping, default-deny egress. **Detective:** the sign-in, port-sweep and beaconing alerts.

**Priorities:** (1) remove the MFA exemption and alert on failures across accounts; (2) block direct outbound HTTPS and DNS so traffic goes through the proxy and resolvers; (3) remove RDP from users to any host and deploy unique local admin passwords. Then DDoS protection, switch protections and fixing the two intranet certificates.
